subject.title: Poem ("O who can ever praise enough...") (The Price)
subject.author: W. H. Auden
subject.text:
POEM
O who can ever praise enough
        The world of his belief?
   Harum-scarum childhood plays
   In the meadows near his home,
   In his woods Love knows no wrong,
  Travellers ride their placid ways,
   In the cool shade of the tomb
  Age's trusting footfalls ring.
O who can paint the vivid tree
        And grass of phantasy?
But to create it and to guard
        Shall be his whole reward.
   He shall watch and he shall weep,
  All his father's love deny,
  To his mother's womb be lost,
  Eight nights with a wanton sleep,
  But upon the ninth shall be
  Bride and victim to a ghost,
And in the pit of terror thrown
        Shall bear the wrath alone.

title: Twenty Lines, Filed as Gossip
standfirst: W. H. Auden wrote this myth of a private world on a wet Saturday in eastern Iceland, buried in a diary-letter about harmoniums and bus fares. It was addressed to Erika Mann, the woman he had married the year before purely to keep her out of Nazi Germany's hands — a day after he copied down a saga's argument that everyone gets to keep a different creed.

sections.heading: Consoled Himself With the Harmonium
sections.body:
By the Saturday he wrote it, Auden had spent most of a week in eastern Iceland tracking his own cold like a weather front — a throat "like a lime kiln" on the Wednesday, a cold that "keeps boiling over like a geysir" crossing a desert road by bus on the Thursday, still "streaming" on the Friday. That Friday he'd also had a bus-ride epiphany about how to structure the whole travel book he was contracted to write, and closed the day's entry musing on his cold's one advantage: "It is a curious fact how often pain or slight illness stimulates the imagination. The best poem I have written this year was written immediately after having a wisdom tooth out."

The next day, rain kept him indoors at a farm near Egilsstaðir. He played the harmonium badly — working through the Air on the G string before coming to grief on a gavotte, diverted along the way by the instrument's stop names: Vox humana, Aeolian harp, Vox seraphicum, Vox celeste, Cor angelicus — then walked out to the bridge over "the half-lake, half-river which fills this valley," Lagarfljót, home in local belief to a lake-worm nobody has ever quite ruled out. He was thinking, he wrote, about "a picture of the seven ages of man I saw in some book or other. A girl playing a flute to a young man, two infants wrestling in a meadow, and an old man staggering to a grave, you know the kind of thing." "After tea," he wrote, "the thoughts developed into a poem."

That poem is the one above it, filed into the diary as one entry among reports on bus fares, herring-gutting at Húsavík, and a fistfight over Icelandic etiquette outside a hotel bar. The letter carrying all of it, day after day, was addressed to his wife.

sections.heading: The Woman He Was Writing To
sections.body:
A year earlier, in June 1935, Auden had married a woman he had never met. Erika Mann was Thomas Mann's eldest daughter, an actress who had spent the early months of Hitler's chancellorship running Die Pfeffermühle, a Munich cabaret that mocked the regime by name until the regime shut it down. By 1935 Germany was moving to strip her of citizenship outright, which would leave her stateless. She asked Christopher Isherwood to marry her; he declined, but suggested Auden. Auden's answer came back by cable, one word: "DELIGHTED." They married at Ledbury Register Office on 15 June 1935, never shared a household, and stayed married and on good terms for the rest of Mann's life — when she died in 1969, her will still named him for a small bequest. That same summer, Auden had also talked his friend John Hampson into marrying Mann's fellow cabaret exile Therese Giehse for the identical reason, and covered the costs himself.

None of that appears in the Iceland letters. What Erika Mann got, week after week, was gossip: bus passengers, harmonium stops, a busload of tourist Nazis on the way to Mývatn "who talked incessantly about Die Schönheit des Islands" and the blond, blue-eyed beauty of Icelandic children — a claim Auden undercuts in the very next sentence, noting that the next two children they passed on the road "were as black as night." In the letters that survive, he never once addresses her as anything but a friend he owes a good story to.

sections.heading: Sigmund's Creed, and Then His Own
sections.body:
The day before the poem, in the same letter, Auden had copied out a story from a Faroese saga. A boy named Sigmund, asked by a woman named Thora to recite the paternoster and creed his foster-father had taught him, sings back a private, patchwork version of his own — built from guardian angels and psalms rather than doctrine. When Thora worries the creed is wrong, a man named Thrand corrects her, not the boy: "Christ, you know, had twelve disciples or more, and each of them had his own credo. Now I have my credo, and you have the credo you have been taught; there are many credos, and they may be right without being exactly the same." Auden transcribed the whole exchange, unglossed, and moved straight on to bus timetables.

Then, one entry later, on the Saturday, he opened his own poem with a version of the same question turned outward: "O who can ever praise enough / The world of his belief?" Not the doctrine everyone is handed — the private one, assembled out of "harum-scarum" childhood, a version of love that "knows no wrong," the trust an old man carries down to the shade of the tomb. The saga hands every believer a credo of his own and calls it fair enough. Auden's poem asks who could ever adequately celebrate the one only he can see.

sections.heading: Not Shakespeare's Seven Ages
sections.body:
The picture Auden named on his walk is recognisably Jaques's speech from *As You Like It* — infant, schoolboy, lover, soldier, justice, old age, one stage replacing the last. Auden's poem refuses that sequence. Its first twelve lines ask the same rhetorical question twice — "O who can ever praise enough / The world of his belief?" and then "O who can paint the vivid tree / And grass of phantasy?" — and each time the answer piles up childhood, love, travel and old age inside the same handful of lines, all present at once rather than arriving in turn: "harum-scarum childhood" in its meadows, love that "knows no wrong" in its woods, travellers passing through, age dying at the same address. (The diary spells it "grass of fantasy"; the poem, once it stood alone in print, was revised to the older spelling, "phantasy.")

It isn't a life stepped through in order. It's a place, made rather than lived through, and the poem is exact about what making it is worth: "to create it and to guard / Shall be his whole reward." Not to inhabit it. To build it, and stand guard.

sections.heading: What the Ninth Night Costs
sections.body:
The second movement doesn't explain what the private world is being guarded against; it just narrates the toll. He shall watch, and weep, and deny his father's love; be lost, somehow, back into his mother's womb; sleep "wanton" for eight nights, and on the ninth become, in the same breath, both "bride and victim to a ghost" — married to and destroyed by the same presence — before being thrown into "the pit of terror" to "bear the wrath alone." None of it resolves into a single myth Auden is quoting from. It reads like the shape of an initiation rite invented on the spot, borrowed piece by piece — a father renounced, a mother's womb, a fixed count of nights, a climactic ordeal — from the vocabulary of rites of passage in general rather than settled on one in particular. What is legible is the bargain underneath it: the private world of the poem's first half, called "his whole reward," is bought in the second half with total isolation.

Auden seems to have agreed with that reading closely enough to act on it. When the poem later stood on its own, printed in *Poetry* magazine in January 1937, stripped of the diary, the buses and the harmonium, it appeared under the title the letter to his wife had never needed: "The Price."
